cases.title: The ozone layer and the Montreal Protocol
cases.oneLine: Every country gains from an intact ozone layer whether or not it pays to protect it; a treaty with a trade ban, payments and a grace period made joining the better move, and nearly all of the banned chemicals are gone.

inPlainWords.players: the 198 parties and the chemical industries they regulate
inPlainWords.cooperate: stop making and using CFCs and halons and pay for substitutes
inPlainWords.defect: keep the cheap chemicals and let everyone else's cuts protect the shared layer
inPlainWords.temptation: the layer is non-excludable: a country that keeps using CFCs still gets the benefit of others' cuts
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: the damage was invisible, decades-long (CFCs last 40-150 years) and fell on everyone, while the cost of switching fell on each user
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: Article 4 banned trade in the chemicals with non-parties, so staying out cost market access; Article 10 and the Multilateral Fund paid developing countries' incremental costs, so joining cost them little; Article 5 gave them ten more years; scientific assessments allowed the rules to be tightened
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For each country: others cut and I do not (temptation) > all cut (reward) > nobody cuts (punishment) > I cut alone (sucker). The trade ban lowers the temptation and the Fund's payments raise the sucker's payoff, until joining is the best reply.

timeline.move: Molina and Rowland publish the warning that CFCs destroy ozone
Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin report large ozone losses over Antarctica
Montreal Protocol adopted; the US signs the same day
US ratifies
Protocol enters into force
Parties must ban imports of CFCs and halons from non-parties
London Amendment: total phase-out of CFCs and halons, financial mechanism for developing countries
Interim Multilateral Fund begins
Multilateral Fund made permanent
Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Crutzen, Molina and Rowland
Kigali Amendment adds the HFC phase-down
Assessment: nearly 99% of banned substances phased out; recovery to 1980 values by about 2040-2066
Record US$965 million replenishment of the Fund for 2024-2026
198 parties

outcome.what: Consumption of CFCs fell from about 1.08 million ODP tonnes (1986) to 2,200 (2009) and below zero net from 2010; nearly 99% of the banned substances are phased out; halogens over Antarctica have fallen 28% of the way back to the 1980 level and over mid-latitudes 55%; the layer is projected to recover around 2040-2066.
outcome.why: Joining was made individually rational: a trade ban on non-parties raised the cost of defection, the Multilateral Fund paid developing countries' incremental costs, a ten-year grace period eased the start, and periodic science assessments let the parties tighten the rules.
outcome.caveats: The ozone hole's yearly size swings with weather; the projected dates assume current policies hold.

cases.payoffShort: a trade ban on non-parties, payments for developing countries' costs, a ten-year grace period

cases.title: Northern cod: the Grand Banks collapse of 1992
cases.oneLine: Canadian inshore and offshore fleets and foreign trawlers all fished one stock; each gained the whole value of its catch and bore only a share of the depletion, and in 1992 the spawning stock was about 10% of its long-term average.

inPlainWords.players: the Canadian inshore fishery, Canadian offshore trawlers, foreign fleets fishing outside the 200-mile limit, and the regulator that set the catch
inPlainWords.cooperate: keep total catch at a level the stock can replace
inPlainWords.defect: take more now, including the young fish, because what one fleet leaves in the sea another may catch
inPlainWords.temptation: a fleet keeps the full value of each extra tonne while the cost, a smaller stock, is shared by all
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: the stock straddled the 200-mile line, harvesting and processing capacity was out of balance with the resource (the 1992 release itself calls for that balance), and stock estimates were uncertain
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: nothing in time: the 1992 moratorium closed the fishery after the collapse; a 1998-2002 inshore fishery had to be closed again in 2003
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For each fleet: others restrain and I fish hard > all restrain > all fish hard > I restrain alone. Without enforceable limits, fishing hard is the best reply whatever the others do, and the stock is the shared loss.

outcome.what: Landings fell from 810,014 t (1968) to 413 t (1995) and the modelled spawning stock from 903 kt (1985) to 10 kt (1995). The fishery stayed closed, apart from 1998-2002, until 2024.
outcome.why: Catch limits stayed above what the stock could bear and fleets inside and outside the 200-mile zone kept fishing; the 2005 parliamentary committee called it overfishing caused by foreign and domestic mismanagement. The 1992 government release had blamed mainly ecological factors.
outcome.caveats: Model estimates (SSB) differ between assessment vintages; the 2018 and 2025 models are not on one scale. Cold water in 1991 and seals are named in the sources as contributing factors.

cases.payoffShort: nothing in time; a moratorium after the collapse

cases.title: Maine lobster: harbor gangs, the V-notch and zone councils
cases.oneLine: Each lobsterman gains by keeping an egg-bearing female that would breed for everyone; territorial harbor gangs, a voluntary V-notch custom backed by law, and elected zone councils made restraint pay; with warmer water helping, landings rose from 5.5 million pounds in 1924 to 132.6 million in 2016.

inPlainWords.players: between about 5,000 and 7,500 license holders since 1988, fishing from harbors along the Maine coast; the state and the interstate commission
inPlainWords.cooperate: notch the tail of an egg-bearing female and throw it back; respect gauges, trap limits and territories
inPlainWords.defect: keep the egged female or the short lobster and sell it; fish another harbor's ground
inPlainWords.temptation: the egged female is worth money today, while its eggs benefit every fisherman on the coast
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: no one can see what happens on another boat; in the 1920s and 1930s laws were widely broken and 40% of fishermen went broke between 1928 and 1930
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: small, closed harbor gangs that know each other and defend territories (boundaries and sanctions); the V-notch law that makes a notched lobster untouchable forever; a belief that conservation works, a long horizon and reputation; from 1995 zone councils elected by license holders set trap limits and entry rules
inPlainWords.formalGame: prisoner's dilemma repeated in small groups
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: The same ordering as the cod, but the players meet daily for decades in closed harbor groups: the shadow of the future (games.json: w at least 1/2 for tit for tat) and reputation make restraint the better long-run strategy, which is Acheson and Gardner's explanation.

timeline.move: State begins buying egged lobsters from pounds and marking them; marked lobsters may not be taken
Bust: 40% of fishermen go out of business; conservation laws widely violated
The mark becomes a V-shaped notch
Zone Management Law: seven zones run by elected councils with their own trap limits
Record landings, 132.6 million pounds
Southern New England's fishery at a record low, 1.7 million pounds
Gauge changes to protect spawners repealed after industry objections
Assessment: not depleted, but overfishing occurring; abundance below the industry target

outcome.what: Landings rose from about 5.5 million pounds (1924) to 132.6 million (2016); since then they fell to 87.3 million (2024) and a preliminary 78.8 million (2025), and the 2025 assessment finds overfishing occurring with abundance below the industry's own target.
outcome.why: Ostrom's conditions hold: clear boundaries (harbor gangs, zones), users making their own rules (zone councils), monitoring and sanctions among people who meet again and again, rights recognised by the state. Acheson and Gardner add belief, a long horizon and reputation. Warm water and few predators helped the boom (Acheson and Gardner); ASMFC says temperature changes have likely played a role in recruitment, and the southern fishery is at a record low.
outcome.caveats: How much of the boom the rules caused, and how much the ocean did, is not settled (the authors say both). Territorial defence includes illegal gear cutting.

cases.payoffShort: closed harbor gangs with territories, the V-notch law, elected zone councils

cases.title: OPEC+: the March 2020 breakdown and the April 2020 cut
cases.oneLine: Each producer gains by pumping above its quota while the others hold back; when OPEC+ failed to agree on 6 March 2020, Saudi Arabia ramped output toward full capacity, Brent averaged $18.38 in April, and on 12 April the group agreed a 9.7 mb/d cut.

inPlainWords.players: OPEC's members and 10 partner countries (OPEC+), led by Saudi Arabia and Russia
inPlainWords.cooperate: hold output at the agreed quota so the price stays high
inPlainWords.defect: produce above quota and sell more barrels at the price the others' restraint holds up
inPlainWords.temptation: a member that cheats gains volume while the cost, a lower price, is shared by all
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: output is hard to observe directly and demand collapsed with the pandemic; Iran, Libya and Venezuela were exempt because of sanctions or instability
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: a punishment phase (a month of price war that hurt every producer), then a deal with a common baseline for the two leaders, a monitoring committee using secondary-source production estimates, and a tapering schedule
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For each member: others hold quota and I cheat > all hold quota > all pump > I hold quota alone. Monthly meetings make it repeated; March-April 2020 was a punishment phase that restored cooperation.

outcome.why: The price war showed every member what defection by all costs (a punishment phase, after which restraint resumed); the April deal gave Saudi Arabia and Russia equal baselines and set up monitoring. Pandemic demand, not only the cartel, drove the price.

cases.title: Silicon Valley Bank, March 2023
cases.oneLine: If no one withdraws, every depositor is safe; if others run, the first to leave gets paid. With 94% of deposits uninsured, $40 billion left SVB on 9 March 2023 and the bank was closed the next day; the government then protected all of SVB's depositors, insured or not, to stop the run spreading.

inPlainWords.players: SVB's depositors, mostly businesses with balances above the insurance limit (94% of deposits were uninsured), the bank, and the agencies that can guarantee deposits or lend
inPlainWords.cooperate: leave the money in and let the bank ride out its securities losses
inPlainWords.defect: wire the money out before others do
inPlainWords.temptation: not a temptation to cheat but fear: a depositor who stays while others run can lose everything above the insured limit (a coordination game, Diamond-Dybvig)
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: deposits were concentrated among a small number of large depositors and most of the money left by wire within the first few days (FDIC, 2026), and the 8 March announcement of a $1.8 billion loss was a public signal
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: deposit insurance and a lender of last resort make staying safe; on 12 March the systemic risk exception covered all SVB deposits and the Fed's BTFP lent against securities at par
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For a depositor: everyone stays > I run while the others stay (I lose a little) and I run when the others run (I save part) > I stay while the others run (I lose what is uninsured). Two equilibria, all stay or all run; a guarantee removes the bad one.

outcome.verdict: the run won at SVB; the guarantee stopped the panic spreading
outcome.what: SVB failed within two days of its announcement; two more banks failed after runs. The guarantee and new Fed lending contained it, at an estimated $20 billion cost to the insurance fund, to be recovered from banks by a special assessment.
outcome.why: Uninsured depositors were in a coordination game with no floor; only a promise that staying is safe (insurance, a lender of last resort) removes the reason to run, as Diamond and Dybvig showed. Insured retail depositors, who had that floor, stayed.
outcome.caveats: Covering uninsured deposits ex post raises moral hazard; the FDIC figures of 2026 pass the gate only if Jev supports them.

cases.title: The UAW Stand Up strike, September-October 2023
cases.oneLine: Each side loses every day the plants are idle and wins by holding out longer; the UAW struck all three Detroit automakers at once but only at chosen plants, widened it six times, from 12,700 to 49,800 workers, and settled by 30 October with 25% base raises.

inPlainWords.players: the United Auto Workers and its members; General Motors, Ford and Stellantis
inPlainWords.cooperate: for workers: stay out together and keep the line; for the companies: settle
inPlainWords.defect: for a worker: cross the line or vote down the strike; for a company: wait the union out, or split the union by settling separately
inPlainWords.temptation: each worker gains from a contract whether or not they bore the strike (a collective-action problem inside the union), and each company hopes the others settle first
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: a long strike costs members their wages and tests their solidarity; the union's public case was that the companies' record profits could pay ('record profits mean record contracts')
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: targeted, escalating strikes: idle a few plants, add more in steps, and reward a company that moves (Ford put 50% more on the table); record profits as the public argument
inPlainWords.formalGame: war of attrition (bargaining with costly delay)
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: Both sides lose every day of the strike; the side that holds out longer wins the larger share. Escalation in steps raises the companies' daily cost faster than the union's.

outcome.why: Escalating, targeted strikes kept the union's cost low and the companies' uncertainty high, and kept members' solidarity cheap; each company could end its losses by settling first.
outcome.caveats: The union's description of its gains is the union's; the BLS counts and Ford's cost are independent.

cases.title: The US debt ceiling standoffs of 2011 and 2023
cases.oneLine: Each side gains if the other swerves first, and a default would hurt both; in 2011 the deal came on 2 August and S&P downgraded the US three days later, and in 2023 the House passed the deal on 31 May, it became law on 3 June, and Fitch downgraded in August.

inPlainWords.players: the House majority and the President, with the Senate, Treasury and bond investors
inPlainWords.cooperate: raise or suspend the limit early, on terms both can accept
inPlainWords.defect: hold out for concessions as the X-date approaches
inPlainWords.temptation: the side that holds out longer wins more of what it wants, as long as the other swerves
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: the cost of crashing (a default) is so large that each side expects the other to give way, and the X-date can only be estimated, so last-minute deals risk default (GAO)
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: nothing structural: each time a last-minute law raised or suspended the limit; GAO recommends replacing the process
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For each side: the other swerves > both swerve (an early deal) > I swerve > nobody swerves (default, the worst for both). Each waits for the other at the brink; a default has never happened.

outcome.verdict: someone always swerved, late and at a cost
outcome.what: No default; the limit has been raised, extended or redefined 78 times since 1960. The 2011 delay cost about $1.3 billion in FY2011; two downgrades followed the 2011 and 2023 standoffs; bills maturing near the X-date were shunned.
outcome.why: Chicken has no stable cooperative outcome without commitment: each side waits for the other at the brink. The game recurs because the limit is set separately from the spending and tax laws that require the borrowing.
outcome.caveats: The 2023 bill-yield inversion also reflects Fed policy; GAO's 2012 and 2026 estimates use different methods and are not additive.

cases.payoffShort: nothing structural; a last-minute law each time

cases.title: The global minimum tax, 2021 and after
cases.oneLine: Each country gains investment and booked profits by taxing companies a little less than its neighbours, and all lose revenue when everyone does; the average statutory rate fell from 28.0% in 2000 to 21.7% in 2019, and in 2021 136 jurisdictions agreed a 15% floor that takes the gain out of undercutting.

inPlainWords.players: about 140 governments competing for multinational companies' profits and investment
inPlainWords.cooperate: tax large multinationals at 15% or more
inPlainWords.defect: undercut to attract profits and headquarters
inPlainWords.temptation: the undercutter gains the tax base others lose
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: profits can be booked where taxes are low with little real activity there (profit-shifting indicators remain far higher in investment hubs)
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: the 15% floor is enforced by top-up taxes: if a low-tax country does not tax its multinationals up to 15%, the parent or other countries may, so undercutting no longer moves the money; a domestic top-up tax (QDMTT) lets the low-tax country collect it first
inPlainWords.formalGame: n-player prisoner's dilemma (race to the bottom)
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For each country: others keep rates and I undercut > all keep rates > all undercut > I keep my rate while others undercut. The top-up tax removes the gain from undercutting below 15%.

timeline.move: Average statutory corporate rate 28.0%

Impact estimate: +US$91-155 billion a year; profit shifting cut by 22.6-44.6%

outcome.verdict: the race halted; the floor is partly built
outcome.what: The average statutory rate stopped falling after 2019 (21.2% in 2025); corporate tax rose to 17.8% of tax revenue in 2022. The US withdrew its support in January 2025; the 2026 Side-by-Side package accommodates comparable minimum-tax systems.
outcome.why: The top-up tax changes the payoffs: undercutting below 15% no longer keeps the revenue away from other countries, so the best reply is to collect it at home. Holdouts lose little by staying out, which is why participation, not the rate, is the weak point.
outcome.caveats: Whether the halt is the deal's effect or began before it (rates were stable from 2019) is not settled by these sources; the 2026 facts pass only through the gate.

cases.payoffShort: a 15% floor enforced by top-up taxes, so undercutting no longer keeps the revenue

cases.title: The US-China tariff war, 2018-2026
cases.oneLine: Each side gains by protecting its producers and pressing the other, and both lose trade when both do; the two answered each other's main tariff rounds, made truces in 2020 and 2025, and in spring 2025 the averages reached 134.3% (US on China, one day in April; 126.1% by early May) and 147.6% (China on the US, mid-April).

inPlainWords.cooperate: keep tariffs low; honour purchase and tariff commitments
inPlainWords.defect: raise tariffs or controls on the other
inPlainWords.temptation: a tariff can win concessions or protect an industry if the other does not respond
inPlainWords.whyItWasHard: each side retaliated (tit for tat), and truces were hard to verify or enforce (China bought 58% of what Phase One promised)
inPlainWords.whatChangedThePayoffs: truces with suspensions and expiry dates (Phase One 2020; Geneva, May 2025; Kuala Lumpur, November 2025); a US court ruling in February 2026 removed one legal tool
inPlainWords.formalGame: iterated prisoner's dilemma between two players
inPlainWords.payoffOrder: For each side: I tariff and the other does not > neither does > both do > the other tariffs and I do not. Their moves look like tit for tat, the strategy that won Axelrod's tournaments (games.json): escalations and de-escalations were both answered in kind.

outcome.what: US imports from China fell from $505.2 billion (2017) to $308.7 billion (2025); average tariffs stood at 35.2% (US on China) and 31.9% (China on the US) on 22 August 2026, against 3.1% and 8.0% in January 2018 (PIIE, in the repository's series).
outcome.why: Both sides played something like tit for tat: the main escalations were answered, and so were the de-escalations (at Geneva both averages were cut at once). Truces held only with deadlines and suspensions; Phase One's purchase promise was, in PIIE's words, problematic if not unrealistic from the start, and was not met.
outcome.caveats: PIIE's averages are statutory rates on fixed 2017 trade, not duties paid; part of the fall in direct imports reflects rerouting through third countries. The series' one-day US high (134.27%, 10 April 2025) is above the 126.1% PIIE's text gives for early May.

facts.claim: The Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987 and entered into force in 1989.
facts.quote: The landmark agreement was signed in 1987 and entered into force in 1989.

facts.claim: The Montreal Protocol was adopted at Montreal on 16 September 1987 and entered into force on 1 January 1989.
facts.quote: Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer Montreal, 16 September 1987 Entry into force : 1 January 1989, in accordance with article 16(1).

facts.claim: As of 4 November 2026 the Montreal Protocol has 198 parties and 46 signatories.
facts.quote: STATUS AS AT : 04-11-2026 … Status : Signatories : 46. Parties : 198.
facts.notes: A status page dated 2026. Whether 198 is every state is not stated on this page and is not claimed.

facts.claim: The United States signed the Montreal Protocol on 16 September 1987 and ratified it on 21 April 1988.
facts.quote: United States of America 16 Sep 1987 21 Apr 1988

facts.claim: From 1 January 1990 every party must ban imports of the Annex A substances (CFCs and halons) from any state that has not joined the Protocol: free riders lose access to the controlled chemicals' trade.
facts.quote: As of 1 January 1990, each party shall ban the import of the controlled substances in Annex A from any State not party to this Protocol.

facts.claim: Developing countries consuming less than 0.3 kg of Annex A substances per head may delay compliance with the control measures by ten years.
facts.quote: Any Party that is a developing country and whose annual calculated level of consumption of the controlled substances in Annex A is less than 0.3 kilograms per capita on the date of the entry into force of the Protocol for it, or any time thereafter until 1 January 1999, shall, in order to meet its basic domestic needs, be entitled to delay for ten years its compliance with the control measures set out in Articles 2A to 2E

facts.claim: The Protocol's financial mechanism, which includes a Multilateral Fund, pays all agreed incremental costs of developing-country parties' compliance, on top of other aid.
facts.quote: The mechanism, contributions to which shall be additional to other financial transfers to Parties operating under that paragraph, shall meet all agreed incremental costs of such Parties in order to enable their compliance with the control measures of the Protocol. … The mechanism established under paragraph 1 shall include a Multilateral Fund.

facts.claim: In 1990 (London Amendment) the parties agreed to phase CFCs and halons out completely and adopted a financial mechanism for developing (Article 5) countries; the interim Multilateral Fund began on 1 January 1991 and became permanent in 1994.
facts.quote: 1990 London Amendment advances Montreal Protocol Parties agree to the total phase-out of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons in addition to the transfer of ozone-friendly technologies and adopted a financial mechanism for Article 5 countries. 1991 Establishment of the interim Multilateral Fund Interim Multilateral Fund was founded on 1 January to aid developing countries in ozone layer protection efforts. … 1994 Multilateral Fund permanently established The Multilateral Fund gains permanent status, becoming the first financial mechanism born from an international treaty.

facts.claim: In 2023 the parties agreed a record replenishment of the Multilateral Fund of US$965 million for 2024-2026.
facts.quote: 2023 Historic replenishment of the Fund A record replenishment of US $965 million is agreed upon, setting a new benchmark for the 2024-2026 triennium.

facts.claim: The Multilateral Fund reports US$4.3 billion in grants for 10,198 approved projects in 144 developing countries.
facts.quote: $4.3 BN In grant funding 10,198 Approved projects 144 Developing countries assisted
facts.notes: A running total on the Fund's home page as read on 4 Nov 2026; the page gives no as-of date, so it is treated as dated 2026.

facts.claim: The Kigali Amendment (2016) added a phase-down of HFCs, the ozone-safe substitutes that are strong greenhouse gases.
facts.quote: The most recent amendment, the Kigali Amendment, called for the phase-down of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) in 2016.

facts.claim: The 2022 quadrennial assessment (presented 9 January 2023) found that nearly 99% of banned ozone-depleting substances had been phased out.
facts.quote: confirms the phase out of nearly 99% of banned ozone-depleting substances has succeeded in safeguarding the ozone layer

facts.claim: If current policies hold, the ozone layer returns to 1980 values around 2066 over the Antarctic, 2045 over the Arctic and 2040 elsewhere.
facts.quote: If current policies remain in place, the ozone layer is expected to recover to 1980 values (before the appearance of the ozone hole) by around 2066 over the Antarctic, by 2045 over the Arctic and by 2040 for the rest of the world.

facts.claim: The Kigali Amendment is estimated to avoid 0.3-0.5 °C of warming by 2100.
facts.quote: The Scientific Assessment Panel said this amendment is estimated to avoid 0.3–0.5°C of warming by 2100 (this does not include contributions from HFC-23 emissions).

facts.claim: At the beginning of 2024 NOAA's Antarctic ozone-depleting gas index was 72 (71.6): reactive halogens had decreased 28% from their peak relative to the 1980 benchmark.
facts.quote: On the ODGI scale, the value of ODGI-A at the beginning of 2024 was 72 (71.6) i.e., by that time reactive halogen concentrations in the Antarctic springtime stratosphere had decreased 28% (i.e., 100-71.6) from their peak relative to the 1980 benchmark halogen value

facts.claim: NOAA's mid-latitude ozone-depleting gas index was 45 (45.3) in 2024: reactive halogens had decreased 55% from their peak relative to the 1980 benchmark.
facts.quote: On this scale, the 2024 value of the ODGI-ML was 45, i.e., by that time reactive halogen concentrations in the mid-latitude stratosphere had decreased 55% (i.e. 100-45.3) from their peak relative to the 1980 benchmark value

facts.claim: Antarctic springtime halogens are projected to return to the 1980 level around 2070.
facts.quote: Reactive halogen concentrations in the Antarctic springtime stratosphere are projected to decline to that 1980 value sometime around 2070

facts.claim: Crutzen, Molina and Rowland received the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on the formation and decomposition of ozone.
facts.quote: 11 October 1995 … for their work in atmospheric chemistry, particularly concerning the formation and decomposition of ozone

facts.claim: On 2 July 1992 Fisheries Minister John Crosbie closed the northern cod fishery with a two-year moratorium.
facts.quote: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE July 2, 1992 Crosbie Announces First steps in Northern Cod Recovery Plan A two-year moratorium on the northern cod fishery was announced on today by John C. Crosbie, Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.

facts.claim: Fishermen and plant workers were offered emergency payments of $225 a week for 10 weeks.
facts.quote: emergency assistance payments of $225 a week will be made for the next 10 weeks to fishermen and plant workers affected by the moratorium

facts.claim: The 1992 release called for a fishery whose harvesting and processing capacity is in balance with what the stock can yield.
facts.quote: take the decisions necessary to create a sustainable northern cod fishery built on a full-time professional work force, as well as harvesting and processing capacity that is in balance with the potential of the resource

facts.claim: In 1992 the spawning cod (age 7+) were estimated at 50,000-110,000 tonnes, about 10% of the long-term average.
facts.quote: The critical estimate of cod seven years old and older, an indicator of spawning potential, is between 50,000 and 110,000 tonnes, among the lowest ever observed and about 10 percent of the long-term average.

facts.claim: The July 1992 federal release attributed the decline since 1990 primarily to ecological factors: it had halved the biomass and cut the spawning biomass by three-quarters.
facts.unit: share of biomass and spawning biomass lost since 1990
facts.quote: Since 1990, a devastating decline in the stock of northern cod off the east coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, due primarily to ecological factors, has reduced the biomass by half and the spawning biomass by three-quarters.
facts.disputed: The government's 1992 attribution to ecology is disputed by the 2005 committee report (cod-2005-overfishing).

facts.claim: Of 1992's 50,000-tonne reference catch, offshore vessels had already taken 15,000 t, foreign vessels outside the 200-mile limit 10,000 t, and 10,000 t was set aside for by-catch, leaving 15,000 t for the inshore.
facts.quote: Already in 1992, 15,000 tonnes have been taken by offshore vessels, approximately 10,000 tonnes have been set aside for by-catches, and another 10,000 have been taken by foreign vessels outside the 200-mile limit, leaving only 15,000 of the 50,000 tonnes for harvest.

facts.claim: The Commons fisheries committee (2005, unanimous) concluded that overfishing, the result of foreign and domestic mismanagement, caused the collapse.
facts.quote: That we conclude that overfishing was the cause of the collapse of the northern cod stock should not surprise anyone. However, in our view, it is clear that overfishing is a consequence of mismanagement, both foreign and domestic

facts.claim: A small inshore fishery reopened in 1998-2002 and was closed again in 2003 because the harvest hit the stock harder than expected.
facts.quote: There was a limited index commercial fishery restricted to the inshore between 1998 and 2002, but the fishery was closed again in 2003 following the realization that the harvest had had a more severe and rapid impact on the resource than expected.

facts.claim: On 26 June 2024 Minister Diane Lebouthillier ended the moratorium, reopening a commercial northern cod fishery with a Canadian TAC of 18,000 t.
facts.quote: June 26, 2024 … Today, the Honourable Diane Lebouthillier, Minister of Fisheries, Oceans, and the Canadian Coast Guard announced the end of the Northern cod moratorium off the north and east coasts of Newfoundland and Labrador. This historic decision re-establishes a commercial Northern cod fishery in NAFO Divisions 2J3KL with a Canadian Total Allowable Catch (TAC) of 18,000 tonnes for the 2024 season.

facts.claim: The stock had been in the Cautious zone since 2016; NAFO's other parties keep 5% of the overall TAC.
facts.unit: % of overall TAC to other NAFO parties
facts.quote: The 2J3KL Northern cod stock has been in the Cautious zone since 2016. … The Canadian TAC of 18,000t is considered 95 per cent of the overall TAC.

facts.claim: In June 2025 the TAC rose from 18,000 t to 38,000 t.
facts.quote: allowing for a responsible total allowable catch (TAC) increase from 18,000 tonnes (t) to 38,000 t.

facts.claim: DFO's 2025 assessment put spawning stock biomass at 524 kt (95% CI 404-678), 2.0 times the limit reference point, with recruitment about 90% of pre-collapse levels and fishing mortality 0.020 in 2024.
facts.quote: The 2025 Spawning Stock Biomass (SSB) is 2.0 (95% Confidence Interval [CI] = 1.2–3.3) times the Limit Reference Point (LRP). … SSB in 2025 is estimated at 524 Kt (95% CI = 404–678 Kt). … corresponding to about 90% of pre-collapse (1954–90) levels. … Fishing mortality (F, ages 5+) has been below 0.05 since 2004 and in 2024 was 0.020 (95% CI = 0.016–0.026).
facts.notes: The 2025 model and its LRP (40% of BMSY) differ from the 2018 model's Blim, so SSB/LRP 2.0 is not on the same scale as the 2018 table's SSB/Blim.

facts.claim: On 12 June 2026 DFO said the stock was in the healthy zone for the first time since the 1992 moratorium and raised the TAC from 38,000 t to 59,000 t.
facts.quote: June 12, 2026 … For the first time since the 1992 moratorium, the latest Northern Cod science indicates the stock is in the healthy zone. … Northern cod: TAC increase from 38,000 tonnes to 59,000 tonnes.

facts.claim: Acheson and Gardner (2011) describe V-notching in Maine as a prisoner's dilemma that gives each fisherman an incentive to avoid the practice.
facts.quote: The genesis of this practice is not easily explained, because V-notching poses a prisoner's dilemma problem that gives fishermen an incentive to avoid the practice.

facts.claim: For most of the 20th century V-notching was voluntary, and many fishermen did it although no one off a boat can see whether its crew notches.
facts.quote: For most of the 20th century, the practice of V-notching was voluntary. … However, many fishermen did so voluntarily even though it is impossible to be certain who was V-notching because what happens on a boat cannot be monitored by anyone who is not on the boat.

facts.claim: Three things explain why cooperation took hold: belief that V-notching works, a low discount rate (the long-run gain beats the one-time gain from defecting), and reputation.
facts.quote: An unusual combination of factors explains the V-notch program: (1) a strong belief among those in the industry that the V-notch is effective in conserving the lobster stock; (2) a low discount rate because the long-term gains from V-notching are higher than the one-time gain from defection; (3) a gain in reputation for those who V-notch.

facts.claim: Fishing rights are local: a newcomer must be accepted by a harbor gang and fishes only its territory (about 200 km2 on average), defended sometimes by cutting intruders' gear.
facts.quote: To catch lobster, a person must gain acceptance by a group of people fishing from one harbor, called a "harbor gang" (Acheson 1988). Once admission is gained, the fisherman can fish only in this group's territory; territories average about 200 km2. They are defended in some cases by the surreptitious destruction of lobster gear (Acheson 1988, 2003).

facts.claim: The V-notch program began in 1917, when wardens were allowed to buy egg-bearing lobsters to stop egg-scrubbing; from 1948 the mark was a V-shaped notch.
facts.quote: The V-notch program began in 1917 when the Maine legislature passed a law allowing the wardens to purchase lobsters that had extruded eggs in pounds to stop the pound owners from scrubbing the eggs off and selling them. … In 1948, the law was changed so that lobsters were marked by a V-shaped notch in the tail rather than a round hole (Laws of Maine 1947).

facts.claim: In the bust of the 1920s and 1930s, 40% of lobster fishermen went out of business between 1928 and 1930; conservation laws were widely violated.
facts.quote: Forty percent of lobster fishermen went out of business between 1928 and 1930 … The low stock sizes were produced, in some part, by the widespread violation of the conservation laws.

facts.claim: The 1995 Zone Management Law split the coast into seven zones run by councils elected by license holders, each with its own trap limits and entry rules.
facts.quote: (5) in 1995, the Zone Management Law, which changed many aspects of lobstering. The Zone Management Law divides the coast into seven zones run by zone councils elected by lobster license holders. This law established an apprenticeship program for the state. The zones have different trap limits and limited-entry rules.

facts.claim: Catches hovered near 7.5 million kg a year from the Second World War to 1989 and exceeded 22.7 million kg in every year after 2000, a boom the authors credit to warm water and few predators working with the conservation rules.
facts.quote: From World War II to 1989, catches hovered around 7.5 million kg per year (Acheson 2003). From 1989 to the present, catches have been at record-high levels despite decades of intense exploitation. In every year after 2000, catches have exceeded 22.7 million kg. This boom is due to environmental factors, e.g., favorable water temperature and low predation by large finfish, working in tandem with conservation laws

facts.claim: Unlike most fisheries, the Maine lobster fishery has repeatedly solved its collective action dilemmas.
facts.quote: The lobster fishery is different in that it has repeatedly solved its collective action dilemmas (Acheson 2003).

facts.claim: ASMFC's 2025 assessment: the Gulf of Maine/Georges Bank stock is not depleted but overfishing is occurring; 2021-2023 abundance (202 million) fell below the industry target (229 million) and stays above the limit (143 million).
facts.quote: Based on these reference points, the GOM/GBK stock is not depleted and overfishing is occurring … The average abundance from 2021-2023 (202 million lobsters) has declined below the fishery/industry target (229 million lobsters) but remains above the abundance limit (143 million lobsters) and abundance threshold (89 million lobsters).

facts.claim: Southern New England's lobster landings fell to a record low of 1.7 million pounds in 2023, 1% of US landings.
facts.quote: SNE landings have continuously declined to the lowest on record in 2023 (1.7 million pounds), now accounting for only 1% of US landings.

facts.claim: ASMFC: lobsters do best at 12-18 °C and are stressed above 20 °C, and temperature changes have likely played a role in the population changes seen in the assessment, such as recruitment.
facts.quote: indicating an optimal range of 12° – 18° C and a threshold for physiological stress at 20°C for adult lobsters. Temperature changes through time have likely played a role in population dynamics observed during the assessment such as changes in recruitment.

facts.claim: Gauge and vent changes triggered in October 2023 to protect spawners were repealed in May 2025 (Addendum XXXII) after industry objections.
facts.quote: Changes were triggered in October 2023 based on observed declines in recruit abundance indices, but these changes were ultimately repealed with the subsequent approval of Addendum XXXII in May 2025 due to lobster industry concern regarding the potential economic impacts of increasing the minimum gauge size

facts.claim: Elinor Ostrom shared the 2009 economics prize for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.
facts.quote: 12 October 2009 … "for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons"

facts.claim: Ostrom's design principles for long-lived commons include clear user and resource boundaries, recognised rights of users to make their own rules, and nested layers of governance.
facts.quote: 1A. User Boundaries: Clear and locally understood boundaries between legitimate users and nonusers are present. … 7. Minimal Recognition of Rights: The rights of local users to make their own rules are recognized by the government. … 8. Nested Enterprises: When a common-pool resource is closely connected to a larger social-ecological system, governance activities are organized in multiple nested layers.

facts.claim: Maine's 2025 landings figures are preliminary, last updated 9 February 2026.
facts.quote: 2025 are preliminary and were last updated 2/9/26.
facts.notes: The landings table PDF itself is footed 'Last Updated 2/6/2026'; the page says 2/9/26.

facts.claim: The OPEC+ meeting of 6 March 2020 ended without agreement on production; on 9 March Brent futures fell below $35, a 24% one-day drop.
facts.quote: On March 9, Brent crude oil front-month futures prices fell below $35/b, a 24% daily decline and the second largest daily price decline on record. Prices fell following the March 6 meeting between members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its partner countries, which ended without an agreement on production levels

facts.claim: After 6 March EIA assumed OPEC would target market share instead of a balanced market: a defection from restraint.
facts.quote: As a result of the outcome of the March 6 OPEC meeting, EIA's forecast assumes that OPEC will target market share instead of a balanced global oil market.

facts.claim: Saudi Arabia ramped production to near full capacity in the second quarter of 2020 after the OPEC+ cuts were suspended in March.
facts.quote: This is a result of Saudi Arabia ramping up its production to near full capacity during the second quarter of 2020, following the suspension of OPEC+ agreed-upon production cuts in March 2020.
facts.notes: Already in the repository as global.json event saudi_russia_price_war (verified 2026-11-03).

facts.claim: On 12 April 2020 OPEC+ agreed to cut 9.7 mb/d from 1 May, tapering to 7.7 mb/d (July-December 2020) and 5.8 mb/d (to April 2022), with Saudi Arabia and Russia each measured from 11.0 mb/d.
facts.quote: Adjust downwards their overall crude oil production by 9.7 mb/d, starting on 1 May 2020, for an initial period of two months that concludes on 30 June 2020. For the subsequent period of 6 months, from 1 July 2020 to 31 December 2020, the total adjustment agreed will be 7.7 mb/d. It will be followed by a 5.8 mb/d adjustment for a period of 16 months, from 1 January 2021 to 30 April 2022. The baseline for the calculation of the adjustments is the oil production of October 2018, except for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and The Russian Federation, both with the same baseline level of 11.0 mb/d.

facts.claim: Compliance is watched: a ministerial committee reviews conformity, measured from secondary-source production estimates.
facts.quote: Reaffirm and extend the mandate of the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee and its membership, to closely review general market conditions, oil production levels and the level of conformity with the DoC and this Statement … Reaffirm that the DoC conformity is to be monitored considering crude oil production, based on the information from secondary sources

facts.claim: OPEC+ is OPEC's members plus 10 non-OPEC partner countries; in 2020 they agreed to cut output as inventories rose quickly in the first quarter.
facts.quote: members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and 10 non-OPEC partner countries, collectively known as OPEC+, agreed to reduce crude oil production in response to rapidly increasing global oil inventories in the first quarter of 2020.

facts.claim: OPEC crude output fell 6.0 million b/d from April to May 2020, the largest monthly decline since 1993; Iran, Libya and Venezuela were exempt.
facts.quote: The U.S. Energy Information Administration's (EIA) monthly data show that OPEC total crude oil production decreased by 6.0 million b/d from April to May, which was the largest monthly production decline since 1993. … OPEC members Iran, Libya, and Venezuela were exempt from the production cut agreement because of economic sanctions or domestic political instability.

facts.claim: On Monday 20 April 2020 the Cushing, OK WTI spot price was -$36.98 a barrel.
facts.quote: Cushing, OK WTI Spot Price FOB (Dollars per Barrel) Week Of Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri … 2020 Apr-20 to Apr-24 -36.98 8.91 13.64 15.06 15.99
facts.notes: EIA daily table row: the week of 20-24 April 2020, Monday first. EIA explains the negative price by low liquidity and scarce storage at Cushing near expiry (opec-negative-why), not by the price war alone.

facts.claim: EIA: WTI futures went below zero on 20 April 2020 for the first time since trading began in 1983, because holders could not find buyers before expiry and storage at Cushing was scarce and costly.
facts.quote: On Monday, April 20, 2020, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil front-month futures traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) were priced in negative dollars per barrel (b) for the first time since trading began in 1983. … The extreme market events of April 20 and April 21 were driven by several factors, including the inability of traders who had purchased futures to find other market participants to sell futures contracts to. In addition, in this case, the scarcity and high cost of available crude oil storage meant several market participants were heavily incentivized to close their positions before having to physically settle their contracts

facts.claim: In October 2022 OPEC+ cut 2 mb/d from November.
facts.quote: Adjust downward the overall production by 2 mb/d from the August 2022 required production levels, starting November 2022

facts.claim: Eight OPEC+ members began returning their 2.2 mb/d of voluntary cuts from 1 April 2025.
facts.quote: they re-affirmed their decision agreed upon on December 5, 2024, to proceed with a gradual and flexible return of the 2.2 mbd voluntary adjustments starting on 1st April, 2025

facts.claim: On 1 March 2026 the eight resumed unwinding the 1.65 mb/d cut of April 2023, adding 206 thousand b/d in April 2026.
facts.quote: the eight participating countries decided to resume the unwinding of the 1.65 million barrels per day of additional voluntary adjustments announced in April 2023 and agreed on a production adjustment of 206 thousand barrels per day. This adjustment will be implemented in April 2026

facts.claim: The UAE announced on 28 April 2026 that it was leaving OPEC from 1 May; without it OPEC's share of world crude output in 2025 would have been 31% instead of 35%.
facts.quote: On April 28, 2026, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) announced that it was leaving OPEC, effective on May 1. … Without the UAE's contribution, the group's share of world total crude oil production would have been 31% in 2025.

facts.claim: SVB grew from $71 billion to over $211 billion in assets in 2019-2021 without heightened standards.
facts.quote: While the firm was growing rapidly from $71 billion to over $211 billion in assets from 2019 to 2021, it was not subject to heightened supervisory or regulatory standards.

facts.claim: About 94% of SVB's deposits were uninsured at the end of 2022.
facts.quote: As of year-end 2022, approximately 94 percent of SVBFG's total deposits were uninsured.

facts.claim: On 8 March 2023 SVB announced it had sold $21 billion of securities at a $1.8 billion after-tax loss and sought $2.25 billion of new capital.
facts.quote: SVBFG had sold $21 billion in available-for-sale (AFS) securities, was booking a $1.8 billion after-tax loss, was planning to increase term borrowings by $15 billion to $30 billion, and was seeking to raise $2.25 billion in capital.

facts.claim: Depositors pulled over $40 billion on 9 March 2023 and $100 billion more was expected the next day; California closed the bank on 10 March.
facts.quote: the bank faced a run by depositors on March 9. Deposit outflows were over $40 billion on March 9, and management expected $100 billion more the next day. This unprecedented outflow led the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (CDFPI) to close the bank on March 10.

facts.claim: On Friday 10 March 2023 California's financial regulator closed Silicon Valley Bank and named the FDIC receiver; the FDIC moved all deposits to a bridge bank it ran.
facts.quote: On Friday, March 10, 2023, Silicon Valley Bank, Santa Clara, CA was closed by the California Department of Financial Protection & Innovation and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) was named Receiver. … To protect depositors, the FDIC transferred all the deposits and substantially all of the assets of Silicon Valley Bank to Silicon Valley Bridge Bank, National Association (N.A.), a full-service bank that was operated by the FDIC.

facts.claim: The Fed's own review: standards were too low and supervision lacked force and urgency.
facts.quote: Regulatory standards for SVB were too low, the supervision of SVB did not work with sufficient force and urgency

facts.claim: On 12 March 2023 Treasury, the Fed and the FDIC invoked a systemic risk exception: all SVB depositors could reach all their money from 13 March; Signature Bank, closed that day, got the same exception.
facts.quote: Secretary Yellen approved actions enabling the FDIC to complete its resolution of Silicon Valley Bank, Santa Clara, California, in a manner that fully protects all depositors. Depositors will have access to all of their money starting Monday, March 13. No losses associated with the resolution of Silicon Valley Bank will be borne by the taxpayer. We are also announcing a similar systemic risk exception for Signature Bank, New York, New York, which was closed today by its state chartering authority.

facts.claim: Losses from covering uninsured depositors were to be recovered by a special assessment on banks.
facts.quote: Any losses to the Deposit Insurance Fund to support uninsured depositors will be recovered by a special assessment on banks, as required by law.

facts.claim: The Fed created the Bank Term Funding Program: loans of up to a year against Treasuries and agency securities valued at par.
facts.quote: The additional funding will be made available through the creation of a new Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP), offering loans of up to one year in length to banks, savings associations, credit unions, and other eligible depository institutions pledging U.S. Treasuries, agency debt and mortgage-backed securities, and other qualifying assets as collateral. These assets will be valued at par.

facts.claim: First-Citizens bought about $72 billion of the bridge bank's assets at a $16.5 billion discount (26 March 2023).
facts.quote: Today's transaction included the purchase of about $72 billion of Silicon Valley Bridge Bank, National Association's assets at a discount of $16.5 billion.

facts.claim: The FDIC estimated the failure's cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund at about $20 billion.
facts.quote: The FDIC estimates the cost of the failure of Silicon Valley Bank to its Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) to be approximately $20 billion.

facts.claim: The 2022 economics prize (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) explained runs as self-fulfilling rumours that deposit insurance and a lender of last resort can prevent.

openQuestions: Nine cases are more than one scene can hold. A first cut of five covers the main games: ozone (public good, solved), cod against lobster (commons lost and kept, drawn side by side), OPEC+ 2020 (cartel and punishment), SVB (run) and the US-China tariffs (iterated dilemma, already in the data). Which does the design keep?
The timeline's 'coded as' labels (cooperate, defect, punish, swerve, escalate) are this research's reading, not the sources'. May the scene colour moves by them, with that stated?

The cause of the cod collapse is disputed: the 1992 federal release says 'primarily' ecological factors, the 2005 Commons committee says overfishing from mismanagement. Show both, or only the committee's later finding?

Who broke OPEC+ on 6 March 2020 is not stated in the cached primary sources (EIA says only that the meeting ended without agreement). Leave it unattributed, or fetch a primary source that names a side?

The CEOs of GM, Ford and Stellantis, the Presidents and Speakers of 2011 and 2023, and the 2025 tariff negotiators are public figures with Wikidata items, but the cached sources do not name their roles; their offices come from Wikidata descriptions. Draw them, or only the named actors (Fain, Yellen, Crosbie, Abdulaziz bin Salman, Novak, Trump, Xi, Cormann, Donohoe)?
Fitch's 2023 wording comes from CNBC because Fitch's page returned no text to a script. Is a secondary source acceptable here, or should that fact stay off screen?
The Russia sanctions coalition and the oil price cap (global.json) are a tenth collective case already gated in the repository. Add it to the scene's set?
PIIE's tariff averages are statutory rates on fixed 2017 trade, not duties paid, and Census trade values do not capture rerouting. Is a caption enough?
